expected_evidence: Geological: elevated concentrations of magnetic/glassy microspherules in a discrete sediment layer dated to ~12,900-12,000 BP (e.g., in lacustrine cores such as those from Lake Cuitzeo, Michoacán, or other Mexican basins)
Geological: associated markers commonly cited for the Younger Dryas Boundary (YDB) layer — nanodiamonds, platinum/iridium anomalies, carbon spherules, soot/charcoal spikes

Astronomical: absence of an impact crater (expected under an airburst mechanism, which typically leaves no crater), so 'evidence' here is more about consistency with airburst physics (e.g., shocked quartz absence, spherule morphology) rather than a crater
Material/archaeological: disruption or abandonment horizons in Paleoindian occupation layers in Mexico coeval with the proposed event; changes in lithic assemblages bracketing the boundary
Genetic: megafaunal extinction signals or population bottlenecks in Mexican fauna coeval with the interval (weak/indirect link)

Model_prior: existing published literature on the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis (Firestone et al. 2007; Israde-Alvarez et al. 2012 for Lake Cuitzeo) and the substantial counter-literature disputing spherule identifications as contamination, fly-ash, or misidentified framboids (Pinter et al. 2011; Daulton et al.)
response.rationale: The interval [-13000,-12001] corresponds to the Younger Dryas onset, so the 'younger-dryas' row is the appropriate detectability reference rather than the unspecified period label. Under that row, geological evidence (0.65) and astronomical evidence (0.7) have relatively high detectability because fine-grained lacustrine and marine sediments from this period are well-preserved globally, including in Mexican lake basins (e.g., Lake Cuitzeo), and such cores have in fact been sampled and analyzed in the real-world YDB literature (model-prior, unverified beyond training recall). Material (0.35) and genetic (0.3) evidence is much less detectable, consistent with sparse Paleoindian archaeological visibility and poor faunal DNA preservation in tropical/subtropical Mexican contexts. Since the mechanism is an airburst, the lack of a crater is expected under the hypothesis itself, not a detectability failure — so absence of crater evidence should not count against the hypothesis. The 'inconclusive' action in the hypothesis is itself consistent with what the detectability profile predicts: moderate-to-good chances of finding candidate geological signatures (spherules, anomalies), but genuine ambiguity in interpretation (contamination, natural framboids, reworking) that plagues this evidence class even when preserved. I weight the aggregate detectability adjustment toward the geological/astronomical end (which carry the actual diagnostic burden for an airburst claim) but pull it down from those individual highs because material and model_prior evidence — needed to contextualize and corroborate the geological signal — are much weaker, and the model_prior evidence available (per my training-derived recall, flagged as low-tier/unverified) indicates unresolved scientific controversy rather than confirmation, which further caps confidence. Overall: evidence of the hypothesized type could plausibly survive and has apparently been sought and reported in Mexico, but detectability is capped at moderate rather than high because (a) diagnostic ambiguity is intrinsic to microspherule/nanodiamond identification, and (b) corroborating material/genetic evidence is weak in this period/region, so an 'inconclusive' finding is a natural and expected outcome rather than evidence of absence.
